summary: Peer roleplay focused on the spouse objection, run before Richard's 1-1 with Chris the same day. Opens with Richard debriefing a bad call — a rescheduled prospect who joined from his car with no camera — and both closers agreeing to study Andrew Musial's recordings, since he is closing and they are not. Michael then plays a prospect who wants to run a $6,000 decision past his wife; Richard isolates the objection down to money and structures a two-payment split live. Michael then introduces a scripted 'responsibility frame' or 'partner tie down' he attributes to Bill Walsh, designed to argue the prospect out of consulting his wife, and the two of them rewrite it for a fitness context, at one point pasting the problem into Claude and reading the output aloud. The recording cuts off mid-sentence as Richard raises a concern about the recordings being pushed into the sales channels.
notable: Michael introduced an externally sourced script, the Bill Walsh 'responsibility frame' or 'partner tie down', whose stated purpose is to make consulting a spouse feel unfair — 'why do you think it's fair for you to actually go to her? Ask her to make a decision on something that she's never really been involved with' and 'what's the decision that he makes right here and right now? And it's probably not go and ask his wife.'
The two closers used a large language model live to rewrite the objection script — 'here's what, I just asked Claude, I don't know if I like this' and 'Yeah, this is what Claude's saying.'

In the roleplay Richard structured a compliant plan live — two payments of $3,000 totalling $6,000 — and framed it as avoiding interest: 'if we split it up into two, so two times 3,000, then it would stay the exact same.' This is the clean structure; contrast the 'six times 1,200' ($7,200) plan described in the same day's team meeting.
Richard is running downsells into the $200/month product: 'he would also be willing to pay 200 a month because this one was going for a downsell.'

Richard's critique of the reported close-rate metric: 'close rate in SalesKick, in Piff Perfect doesn't really make sense, because it doesn't count disqualifies... if you have a disqualified, it's still a taken call.' This sits alongside the same day's team meeting, where unpaid deposits were counted as closed units.

Richard's read on why Andrew is closing and he is not: 'He's having good conversations with them. I think that's it... It doesn't seem like he really has a protocol to solve [objections] or something. He just walks around with him.'

Richard took a call from a prospect sitting in his car who refused to turn on his camera, after a double-booking forced a reschedule, and described it as 'the most awkward conversation I've ever had.' That call does not appear in this batch.
The file ends mid-sentence at the moment Richard says 'It's annoying that these recordings go directly back into the sales channels.'
